claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain and toughness than commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
The improved plastic strain and toughness are caused by the alloy's nanocrystalline structure and high lattice distortion.
Nanocrystallinity and lattice distortion shift deformation from conventional dislocation slip to grain-boundary-mediated plasticity.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr is a single-phase BCC alloy.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a nanocrystalline grain size on the order of tens of nanometers.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has significant lattice distortion.
Atomic-size and modulus misfit among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces lattice distortion.
The nanocrystalline grain structure provides a high density of grain boundaries.
Nanocrystalline WTaTiVZr promotes grain-boundary sliding and intergranular deformation at high temperature.
Coarse-grained pure tungsten instead deforms through localized dislocation slip and brittle fracture under the proposed conditions.
Redistributing strain across many grain boundaries enhances plastic-strain capacity and toughness.
At 800–1000 °C, WTaTiVZr should show higher strain to failure and toughness than pure tungsten.
Deformed WTaTiVZr should exhibit distributed deformation and microstructural evidence of grain-boundary sliding.
Intergranular fracture patterns would constitute evidence of grain-boundary sliding in the WTaTiVZr alloy.
Pure tungsten should show limited plasticity, lower toughness, localized dislocation structures, and early crack initiation under the same conditions.
Grain-boundary-mediated deformation in this alloy is typically activated above 800 °C.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanocrystalline grain size is retained and significant grain growth or phase separation is absent.
Dynamic recrystallization or grain growth during prolonged high-temperature exposure may alter the deformation mechanism.
